Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE); Liam Chen (Redwood SE); Mike Alvarez (AstraVox CTO); Jenna Park (AstraVox SRE); Tom Briggs (AstraVox ML Eng)

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Patel: ok, hi everyone thanks for joining on a Thursday afternoon. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Mike Alvarez: Mike here, yeah thanks. Jenna and Tom are on from infra and ML.
[00:11] Jenna Park: hi all, Jenna.
[00:13] Tom Briggs: Tom here.
[00:15] Liam Chen: Hey team, Liam from Redwood, lead SE on the pilot.
[00:19] Sofia Patel: Great. Agenda: look at the microburst results, dig into TTFT outliers, discuss kernel picks we tried last week, and align next steps. Any other items?
[00:29] Mike Alvarez: I wanted to confirm we're still targeting that 120ms P95 for short answers, anything above that folks see degrade in UX.
[00:36] Tom Briggs: yes, our product team says 100–120ms feels acceptable. Longer is okay for long completions.
[00:41] Liam Chen: noted. We ran three kernel configs — tensor-core optimized, conservative generic kernel, and a hybrid path that hedges by sequence length. I'll pull up the bench highlights.
[00:50] [00:50] Liam Chen: Alright so slide one, microburst A: 100 concurrent single-turn requests, seqlen 16. Tensor core path gave us median ~45ms, P95 ~110ms, microburst tail spikes to 200ms on a cold KV cash miss. The hybrid reduced those spikes to ~140ms P95 by preferring generic kernels for short batch cases.
[01:18] Tom Briggs: wait did you say KV cash? we saw a lot of cache misses in our runs, maybe our request pattern is not primed.
[01:24] Liam Chen: yes, KV cash — sorry, KV cache. The transcription later shows cash — the audio is bad. But real issue is cache priming. We saw heavy variance if the model cache isn't prepopulated.
[01:33] Jenna Park: that's consistent with what we saw on-prem when traffic bursts after idle windows.
[01:38] Mike Alvarez: Can we quantify how much priming helps for short answers?
[01:41] Liam Chen: in our bench priming with warm KV reduced P95 by ~30–40ms on seqlen 16 tests. For seqlen 64 the benefit was smaller, more of a steady improvement.
[01:52] Sofia Patel: Great. On the dedicated vs hosted question — Mike, you asked about cost and SLO guarantees. We're going to send a committed capacity delta. But to pick the right kernel path we should understand your traffic distribution. Tom, do you have that?
[02:07] Tom Briggs: yeah, quick rough: 70% of requests are short (<=32 tokens), 20% mid (33–128), 10% long (>128). During peak events short requests jump to 85%.
[02:20] Liam Chen: that distribution pushes us to optimize for short seqlen performance and TTFT. Hybrid strategy that routes short requests to a specialized tensor-core kernel with aggressive KV priming looks promising, but we saw microburst tail risk if the KV is cold.
[02:35] Mike Alvarez: so that means extra warming? More memory? What's the operational cost?
[02:40] Liam Chen: priming increases token cost slightly and uses more KV capacity—basically more RAM on the serving nodes. But it keeps P95 down. The alternative is hedging: if latency threatens SLO, route to a slightly cheaper model variant with smaller context and that gave us stable P95 at cost of few tokens of context loss.
[03:01] Jenna Park: can you define "slightly cheaper"? we need numbers to weigh.
[03:04] Sofia Patel: yes — we'll include a cost delta. For example, in our bench runs the tensor-core path with priming raised unit cost ~12% vs unprimed generic kernel, while hedging to a smaller variant reduced cost ~8% but increased hallucination risk for certain prompts.
[03:22] Tom Briggs: hallucination risk is a concern for our regulatory docs flow. We can't sacrifice much accuracy there.
[03:27] Mike Alvarez: agreed. Security question: if we go Dedicated or Private, what KMS/HSM options exist and does Redwood support our HSM provider?
[03:36] Liam Chen: we support standard cloud KMS integrations and can integrate with customer HSM via Redwood Private. We'll send the integration notes and our SOC2 artifacts. For Dedicated we can enable customer-managed keys (CMK) and limited key-wrapping flows.
[03:48] Jenna Park: procurement will want details — SSO/SAML, RBAC controls, log retention for audit.
[03:54] Sofia Patel: yes, security pack link included in header. We also have audit-log options with per-token metadata.
[03:59] [04:00] Liam Chen: Back to latency: we noticed sequence-length correlated kernel selection logic was triggered incorrectly when sequence length estimation was off for streaming calls. Some of your streaming traffic has variable tokens mid-stream and our estimator picked the wrong kernel early in the handshake. That produced mid-request kernel swap and fragments, increasing latency.
[04:25] Tom Briggs: that matches our telemetry where the stream handshake seemed to pick the heavy weight path and then switch. Is there a way to re-evaluate mid-stream without penalty?
[04:33] Liam Chen: we can do lightweight sampling: do fast early estimates for the first 8–16 tokens and then decide. There's a tradeoff of a few extra ms on first token to avoid expensive swaps later.
[04:43] Mike Alvarez: so that's a tunable knob — extra ms up-front vs overall tail. We're happy to take 5–10ms if it reduces tail by 40–50ms.
[04:52] Sofia Patel: noted. For the microburst test matrix we propose three runs this week: warm-KV tensor-core baseline, cold-KV tensor-core (to quantify cold penalty), and hybrid early-sampler with mid-stream re-eval. Liam will run.
[05:04] Tom Briggs: when you say cold-KV do you drop cache across nodes or just for a fraction of keys?
[05:09] Liam Chen: we simulate both. Cold across nodes gives worst-case; partial drop simulates churn. We'll include both in the results.
[05:16] Jenna Park: how do these maps look for the Dedicated burst model? If we hit a concurrent load we need autoscaling behavior and warm-up characteristics.
[05:24] Liam Chen: Dedicated gives you reserved pools and faster allocation. Autoscaling still exists but you can pick a warm reserve. For spikes above capacity we have fallback routing to the hosted pool or to smaller model variants per the routing policies.
[05:37] Mike Alvarez: fallback to hosted — does that mean data leaves our VPC?
[05:41] Sofia Patel: good point. In Dedicated we can configure routing to a Redwood-hosted pool but with encryption-in-transit and data retention policies. If you require strict residency, we can instead route to a private pool in your VPC (Redwood Private) but that has longer procurement lead time.
[05:58] Tom Briggs: procurement lead time estimate?
[06:00] Sofia Patel: Private on-prem options typically 8–12 weeks depending on network and HSM integration; Dedicated is weeks, usually 2–4 to provision reserved capacity.
[06:09] Jenna Park: ok. For the TTFT metric specifically, can you demonstrate the first byte/first token breakdown per kernel?
[06:15] Liam Chen: yes — our bench has per-token breakdown. For tensor-core with warm KV: first token serialization ~10–12ms, model exec ~30ms, network overhead ~5ms. For generic kernel model exec was ~55–60ms for similar seqlen. Those numbers change with seqlen.
[06:33] Mike Alvarez: do you have logs or traces we can plug into our tracing system?
[06:36] Liam Chen: yes we can provide open tracing hooks and a sample trace so you can correlate.
[06:40] [06:40] Tom Briggs: about model variants — you mentioned hedging to a smaller model for burst protection, how does that affect quality in our documents compare tests?
[06:50] Liam Chen: hedging to a smaller variant reduces context window and can trim subtle factuals. In our eval on your prompt set it increased factual regression about 2–3% on high-precision prompts. For regulatory content that's material, so for those flows we recommend pinning to the full model and using capacity reserve rather than hedging.
[07:10] Mike Alvarez: ok, so for our regulatory flow we pin and for chat-like short queries we can hedging. That sounds workable.
[07:17] Sofia Patel: quick note on telemetry: please send a sample of the traffic shape (Tom) and we'll map cost + latency curves for three modes: unprimed generic, tensor-core primed, and hybrid queue/hedge.
[07:29] Tom Briggs: will do. I'll attach a week of production-sim traffic.
[07:33] Jenna Park: procurement will need a contract addendum for Dedicated burst and a runbook for failover.
[07:39] Sofia Patel: we have a template — I'll attach.
[07:42] [07:42] Mike Alvarez: Are there any parting gotchas we should be aware of?
[07:46] Liam Chen: one gotcha: quantization choices impact kernel performance. If you choose int8 quant with certain kernels you can see faster exec but worse accuracy on some prompts; another is that sequence-length aligned batching helps but only if your incoming request sizes are stable.
[08:01] Tom Briggs: about quant — we run some evals internally that are sensitive; we can share the eval set.
[08:05] Liam Chen: please do. We'll run quant-variant A/Bs on those.
[08:09] Sofia Patel: ok let's summarize and assign next steps.
[08:12] Sofia Patel: Recap: Redwood to run three targeted microburst runs (Liam), include cold vs warm KV, and hybrid early-sampler. Redwood to share cost delta for Dedicated vs Hosted and pilot amendment (Sofia). Customer to share traffic distribution and eval set for quant tests (Tom). Customer procurement to share SSO/KMS contacts (Jenna).
[08:34] Mike Alvarez: timeline fine. We aim to decide early Oct.
[08:38] Jenna Park: I'll share procurement contacts by Friday.
[08:41] Tom Briggs: uploading traffic sample today.
[08:44] Sofia Patel: Great. Any final questions?
[08:46] Mike Alvarez: none from me. Thanks for the clear plan.
[08:49] Liam Chen: thanks all. We'll follow up in the bench doc and drop raw traces.
[08:55] Sofia Patel: End call.
